rv.q: Don't be put off by any grumbles about the conversational, tightened two-hour adaptation that the Manhattan Theatre Club uses for the rare Broadway production of this timely classic.
This dynamic comes to the fore in Doug Hughes's complex and richly acted production at Manhattan Theatre Club.
Clearly, MTC has lucked out with its timing of this classic drama, its Victorian-era polemics ordinarily a bit simplistic — but given the peculiar insanity of election politics, right on the money.
Mr. Gaines takes confident advantage of this prized chance, giving a sterling performance that allows us to see Dr. Stockmann from all the perspectives Ibsen intended.
But while the broad approach to the material certainly lacks subtlety, it does full justice to both its powerful urgency and frequent doses of mordant humor.
Up until intermission, "An Enemy of the People" seems like your run-of-the-mill Roundabout period revival.
But this 1882 play by Ibsen, a pioneer in realism, has never seemed more simplistic and black-and-white than in this version.

Rebecca Lenkiewicz has transformed Henrik Ibsen's 1882 play "An Enemy of the People," an insightful work about the cost of free expression, into a coherent, topical, and thrilling piece that pokes and prods at our own moral fiber.
"An Enemy of the People" makes for exciting, politically-charged theater.

This Manhattan Theatre Club production also has a huge asset in leading man Boyd Gaines, whose Thomas is a distinctly earthbound but still mesmerizing force of nature -- by turns formidable, frail, frazzled, funny and tragic.
The most serious flaw of this handsome, classical production is that it burns a bit too hot.
As the townsfolk scream down the doctor's cries of concern, I found the play extremely relevant, considering the debate that's raging about how fracking effects our environment.
Richard Thomas does everything but twirl his mustache as the bogeyman in the Broadway revival of 'An Enemy of the People.'
The problem with that, aside from meshing his contradictions into a single, recognizable human being, is that it sticks out of the play like a sore thumb.
In a riveting production by Rebecca Lenkiewicz at the Manhattan Theatre Club, Boyd Gaines plays Dr. Thomas Stockmann who insists on telling the truth though it may cost his livelihood.

cn.t: Ibsen's timely drama about truth versus self-interest gets a high-intensity revival led by strong performances from Boyd Gaines and Richard Thomas, though some critics find the production overly amped-up and lacking restraint.

vs.sum: The Samuel J. Friedman Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions and a well-raked mezzanine, ensuring a clear view from most seats. The sound quality is consistently praised, and the seating is comfortable with decent legroom. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its elegant design following renovation, though facilities like restrooms are average, leading to some congestion during intermissions.

acc.note: Elevator to all levels. Built-in induction loop for t-coil hearing aids.
